entries.old: datawake: Shawna Delgado, Emergency Management Director — Weekly Report, Cycle 116. **Weather.** Cycle 116 came in mild, 54 degrees, impact 1, no advisories and no alerts. This is the sixth consecutive clear cycle. There is nothing on the city's weather event ledger for the cycle and nothing on the crisis-event ledger set moving by weather. Operationally, that is the whole story: a quiet week. **Crisis arcs.** One arc remains open. The Downtown Transit Snarl is in decline — tension 2.45, down from where it has been, easing but still strained. It has been in this phase since Cycle 115 and open since Cycle 114. The item I would keep in front of the council is the underlying housing pressure in Downtown: 10.00 against a citywide figure of 2.52. Our transit picture is improving; the pressure driving people onto and off those routes is not. I would not close the arc while that ratio stands where it does, and I'd expect it to be the thing that reopens the snarl if anything does. **Shock and pattern flags.** Shock flag: none. Pattern flag: none. Civic load: minor-variance. I read that as the city absorbing the week without displacement. **What I am watching into Cycle 117.** First, whether Downtown's tension continues to fall now that it has held a full cycle in decline — a second cycle of easing would let me start talking about an exit condition. Second, the streak. Six clear cycles is good news and also the point where I start watching the other direction; a run this long tends to end with a single high-impact event rather than a gradual one, and my office's readiness posture should not drift just because the ledger is empty. I have nothing to move on that this cycle — no event, no advisory — so this is a note, not a call to action. **Bottom line for the record:** no active weather threat, no new crisis events, one crisis arc easing under persistent housing strain, citywide civic load within minor variance. Nothing in this cycle requires a mayoral decision or a public advisory from this office. That is my report for Cycle 116.

entries.old: datawake: **Fire Chief's Weekly Report — Cycle 116** One engine run this Cycle, in Koreatown (KONO): a major blaze, contained. No loss of life reported, and the block's own account is what I'd expect from a working fire — smoke over the rooftops and the smell of it lingering for days. "Contained" is the word that matters here; it means the fire stopped where we stopped it, but it does not mean the block is done with it. What I'm watching: this is the second time in sixteen Cycles that KONO has shown up in my records — Cycle 100 was a false alarm, no outcome beyond a wasted run. So I won't pretend there's a pattern in the dispatch data; two lines on a sheet is not a trend. But KONO's profile is worth saying out loud all the same. It's a growth neighborhood right now, mild inflow, housing pressure at 1.5, and eleven businesses packed in with the Fox Theater, the galleries and the studios — the arts corridor. Dense blocks with old commercial stock and nightlife traffic are where a contained blaze starts, and they're where it comes back. My people will be back on that block this week checking exposures and talking to the shop owners, because smoke in the walls and a damaged service panel are how a contained fire becomes next month's structure fire. My ask is the usual one, and I'll keep asking it: give my inspectors the access. If a tenant in KONO has a back room off the alley or a stairwell that's been used for storage since the last time anyone looked, I want to see it before the engine does. The neighborhood's sentiment reads 0.05, down 0.06 from where it sits otherwise — a block that smelled smoke and lost a night's sleep. I take that as a bill we owe them, not a complaint. That's the record for Cycle 116. One blaze, contained, in Koreatown. We'll be on the block.
